title: Facade and Flyweight
idea: Facade gives a busy subsystem one simple front door. Flyweight shares one immutable object among many users, so look-alikes store only what differs.
points: A facade class holds the subsystem parts and calls them in the right order.
Callers depend on the facade only, so the parts can change behind it.
Shared intrinsic state, like an icon, stays apart from per-object extrinsic state, like position.
A factory caches flyweights by key and hands back the same instance each time.

messages.label: placeOrder("lamp", 25.0)
messages.note: The caller makes one call. It knows nothing about the three parts.

messages.label: reserve("lamp")
messages.note: The facade checks stock first, because charging for missing goods is wrong.

messages.label: true
messages.note: Stock says yes, so the facade may go on.

messages.label: charge(25.0)
messages.note: Next it charges the customer and keeps the payment id.

messages.label: book("lamp")
messages.note: Then it books a pickup and gets a tracking id.

messages.label: "placed: …"
messages.note: The caller gets one result. The order of steps lives in one place.

code.title: Facade
code.caption: `Checkout` hides three classes and their order behind one method.

walk.text: Three subsystem classes, each with its own small job and its own method.
The facade receives the parts through its constructor and keeps them `private final`.
`placeOrder` owns the sequence and stops early when stock is missing.
`main` wires the parts once, then only ever talks to `Checkout`.

code.title: Flyweight
code.caption: Four map markers share two `Style` objects. Only the position is stored per marker.

walk.text: `Style` is the flyweight: immutable, so sharing it is safe.
`Marker` keeps its own position and a reference to a shared style.
`StyleCache` builds a style once per key and returns the cached one after.
`main` asks for `cafe` three times and compares two styles with `==`.

pitfalls: Keep the facade thin: it orders calls, it should not absorb the subsystem's rules.
Never put mutable state in a flyweight; one change would alter every user.
Skip Flyweight until you have many objects and measured memory pressure.

quiz.q: What does the last line print?
quiz.why: The cache keys on icon and colour. `cafe/brown`, `cafe/red` and `park/green` are three distinct keys; the repeat reuses one.

takeaway: Facade simplifies access to many parts; Flyweight shares state to save memory.

starters: Is a service class in Spring just a facade?
Is Java's string pool an example of Flyweight?
